progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, reduce biodiversity loss and maintain ecological integrity by including all
territory in spatial planning and ensuring effective management.
reportedActions:
To reduce biodiversity loss and maintain ecological integrity, Mongolia continues
efforts to integrate all land areas into spatial planning and ensure effective
management. As a priority, data and information related to internationally
significant rare and endangered species of flora and fauna, ecosystems, water
resources, and wetlands are being systematically consolidated and incorporated
into relevant national and international databases. Within the framework of Key
Biodiversity Areas (KBAs), a total of 69 sites covering 9,908,605 hectares have
been identified and registered in Mongolia. Of these, 25 sites covering 7,686,384
hectares are located within nationally designated protected areas. In addition, 70
Important Bird Areas (IBAs) covering 7,906,557 hectares have been identified (),
of which 69 sites have been assessed under Criterion A1.
In 2025, Mongolia prepared and submitted its National Report under the Ramsar
Convention. A total of 11 wetland sites, covering 1,439,530 hectares, were
designated as wetlands of international importance for water resources,
wetlands, and waterbirds. Of the 11 wetlands listed under the Ramsar List, 8
sites are located within nationally designated protected areas.

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, restore at least 30 percent of degraded ecosystems and improve ecological
integrity and connectivity.
reportedActions:
Mongolia is focusing on the restoration of degraded ecosystems by implementing
land
protection
and
reclamation
activities.
In
2024,
a
total
of 3,673,616.02
hectares nationwide were covered by land protection and restoration measures;
however,
this
represents
a
decrease
of 222,138.14
hectares compared
to
the
previous year. A detailed breakdown of the 2024 restored areas is as follows:
• Pastureland: 3,141,337.8 hectares
• Forest area: 246,253.77 hectares
• Agricultural land: 175,032.10 hectares
• Water area: 56,517.78 hectares
• Urban settlements: 26,884.17 hectares
• State Special Purpose land: 22,567.01 hectares

• Mining land reclamation: 1,790.5 hectares
• Roads and infrastructure networks: 67.89 hectares
In 2024, out of the total 175,032.10 hectares of agricultural land where protection
and restoration measures were implemented, 108 hectares specifically involved the
restoration of severely eroded farmland and abandoned (fallow) lands.
Additionally, protection and restoration efforts were applied to 3,141,337.8 hectares
of pastureland in 2024. This accounts for 85.5% of the total land area covered by
such measures nationwide and represents an increase of 398,798.49 hectares
compared to the previous year.
Since the majority of Mongolia's degraded ecosystems consist of pasturelands, a
nationwide network of research and monitoring plots was established in 2015 to
assess rangeland status. As of 2025, this network has expanded to 5,333 monitoring
points. To support this, several provincial and soum-level Citizens' Representative
Commitees have formally adopted and enforced “Regulations on Accountable
Pastureland Use”.
According to 2021 data, the implementation of sustainable management practices
through the photomonitoring program resulted in the recovery of 20.6 million
hectares of healthy pastureland. Furthermore, under the ENSURE project
(2019–2025), five-year rangeland management plans were implemented in the Gobi
region. As a result, 23.4% of participating herders reduced their livestock numbers,
successfully lowering the grazing pressure on the land.
Within the framework of mining concession protection and reclamation, the following
activities were completed in 2024: 2,165.26 hectares of excavated and degraded
land were backfilled and leveled, 1,769.48 hectares underwent biological
reclamation (revegetation), and 1,020.64 hectares of riverbanks were restored and
their natural flows reinstated.
Regarding urban settlements and villages, protection and restoration efforts in 2024
included: 25,919.19 hectares planted with trees and shrubs, and 28.65 hectares of
topsoil restoration and landscaping (lawns).
Under the initiative of the President of Mongolia, U. Khurelsukh, the "One Billion
Trees" national movement was launched in 2021. The program is being successfully
implemented, with 84 million trees planted as of 2024. These reforestation and
forest restoration efforts are strategically directed toward several key environmental
goals:
• Agricultural Land Restoration: Protecting and reclaiming farmland from
degradation.
• Water Resource Protection: Conserving river basins, riparian zones, and
water sources.

• Mining Reclamation: Restoring land affected by mining activities.
• Forest Restoration: Rehabilitating degraded forests and expanding forested
areas.
• Urban Greening: Increasing green spaces within cities and settlements.
To enhance reforestation and afforestation efforts and prevent forest degradation,
the "Regulations on Forest Treatment and Cleaning" were updated and approved in
2020. Additionally, the cost norms for afforestation and forestry activities were
revised in 2021.
Figure 1. Map of the Forest distribution in Mongolia (2024)[1]
[1] Forest resource of Mongolia. National Forest Agency, 2024.
In the field of peatland protection and restoration, international researchers launched
a five-year project in 2024, with plans to restore 20,000 hectares of peatlands.

Figure 2. Map of peatland distribution in Mongolia[2]
[2] Highland Peatlands of Mongolia, Tatiana Minayeva, Andrey Sirin, Chultemiin
Dugarjav. 2024.
Within the framework of restoring dried up and depleted lakes and ponds, several
lake restoration projects have been implemented. For instance, in the territory of
Delgerkhaan soum, Khentii aimag, the water volume of the Avarga Toson Lake—which
is of exceptional medicinal significance—had decreased by 60% as of 2022 compared
to 1970 levels[1]. Consequently, restoration work was carried out, and measures to
protect and restore the lake and its surrounding shores were implemented[2].
Additionally, between 2021 and 2023, the project "Mitigating Desertification in the
Darkhad Depression and Restoring Tsoitson Lake in Renchinlkhumbe Soum" was
successfully implemented. Starting in 2021, a 403-meter dam was constructed on
the Khodon River using engineering solutions, and a flow-diversion channel was
excavated. As a result, the Khodon River began flowing 10.6 km along its original
course to feed Tsoitson Lake, which was fully restored by 2023. Consequently,
Tsoitson Lake is now capable of storing 35 million cubic meters of water[3].

Mongolia has set a target to restore at least 30% of its degraded ecosystems by 2030.
Furthermore, the country aims to increase its forest cover to 9% of the total land area.
These indicators are directly linked to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs),
specifically:
• Goal 15: Life on Land (Protecting terrestrial ecosystems).
• Goal 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities (Increasing green spaces in
urban settlements).
• Goal 13: Climate Action (Mitigating the impacts of climate change).
At the national level, these objectives are integrated into "Vision 2050," Mongolia’s
long-term development policy.
Additionally, the Government of Mongolia approved the "New Recovery Policy" in
2021. This policy includes a dedicated pillar for Green Recovery, incorporating
strategies to mitigate climate change, expand forest cover, develop agro-forestry,
and protect riparian forests and water sources.

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, 30% of the country's total area will be included in the special protected area
network, representing major ecosystem types and strengthening ecological connectivity.
reportedActions:
For Target 3, Mongolia’s main challenges are the remaining gap to reach 30%
protection by 2030 (an additional ~13.9–14.2 million ha needed), limited ecological
connectivity because many protected areas are isolated, and low coverage of some
key ecosystems (notably steppe and peatlands, and some river headwaters/forest
zones). Further implementation can prioritize expanding protection in under-
represented ecosystems and key connectivity areas, strengthen ecological corridor
planning, increase management effectiveness (staffing/equipment and operational
budgets), improve inclusive buffer-zone governance (including herders, women and
youth), and harmonize protected area data and boundaries across national systems
while scaling sustainable financing mechanisms.
Discrepancies in the numerical data indicate a need to strengthen policy coherence
and improve alignment among the relevant laws and regulations. Mongolia is
pursuing the objective of placing 30% of its territory under protection by 2030 (in
line with the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework). As of 2025,
coverage has reached 21%, suggesting that the country is broadly on track toward
this target. However, substantially accelerated action will be required during
2026–2030 to designate an additional 14 million hectares as protected areas, while
ensuring that new designations adequately represent Mongolia’s major ecosystem
types (i.e., improving ecosystem representativeness and coverage).

Implementation of Target 3 (expanding and effectively managing protected and
conserved areas and strengthening ecological connectivity) relates strongly to SDG
progress because it secures larger, better-connected areas that maintain ecosystem
functions, reduce habitat fragmentation, and safeguard key biodiversity areas and
ecological processes. By strengthening ecological connectivity and management
effectiveness, Target 3 supports long-term ecosystem integrity and resilience across
landscapes.
For the Sustainable Development Goals, Target 3 contributes most directly to SDG 15
(Life on Land)—especially SDG 15.1 (conservation, restoration and sustainable use of
terrestrial and inland freshwater ecosystems) and SDG 15.4 (conservation of
mountain ecosystems), because Mongolia’s protected area system covers extensive
terrestrial and mountain landscapes and aims to improve representativeness and
effectiveness through expansion and better management. It also supports SDG 6.6
by strengthening protection of water-related ecosystems (e.g., headwaters, wetlands
and lakes within protected and conserved landscapes), which helps maintain water
regulation functions and ecosystem services.

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, Reduce the risk of extinction of threatened species and conserve genetic
diversity
reportedActions:
In Mongolia’s long-term strategic framework, the “Vision 2050” program and the
Government Action Program include the following objective: “Revise and establish
updated Red Lists for animal and plant species, define and implement measures
for the conservation of threatened species, conduct phased nationwide surveys of
species
distribution
and
populations,
and
create
conditions
for
implementing
appropriate management”.
Mongolia is actively implementing conservation measures in accordance with a
variety of national laws, such as the Law on Environmental Protection, the Law on
Fees for Natural Resources use, the Law on Environmental Impact Assessment, the
Law on Animal, the Law on Natural Plants, the Law on Plant Health and Protection,
and the Law on Genetic Resources, to reduce the extinction risk of threatened and
endangered species and preserve genetic diversity. Relevant international treaties
and conventions, including the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Convention
on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), the
Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals, and Ramsar
Convention on Wetlands, also guide conservation activities. These national legal
frameworks have been continuously amended and updated in response to the
growing demands for environmental, economic, and societal conservation. For
instance, the Law on Natural Plants was amended eight times between 1997 and
2024, and the Law on Animal was amended seven times between 2015 and 2025.
These amendments were made in conjunction with ongoing endeavors to modernize
the
broader
environmental
legal
framework.
Legislation
in
Mongolia
explicitly
specifies the protection of specific species that are considered endangered. At
present, the legal registry comprises the following:
Plants: 133 vascular plants that are critically endangered and 355 vascular plants
that are endangered; 11 lichens; 5 algae; 4 mosses; and 5 fungi.

Animals: 31 species that are critically endangered and 70 species that are
endangered.
These
data
suggest
that
Mongolia
has
implemented
a
comprehensive
legal
framework to safeguard critically endangered and imperiled species on a national
scale.
In order to safeguard the genetic diversity of microorganisms, plants, and animals,
the Government of Mongolia established a Gene Bank and, in 2022, implemented
regulations to enhance the collection, documentation, preservation, protection, and
distribution of genetic resources. The Law on the Livestock Genetic Resources was
enacted in 2017 to protect livestock genetic resources and preserve genetic diversity.
From 2019 to 2025, it was amended and updated. In addition, the Law on Seeds and
Varieties of Cultivated Plant was revised and amended in 2021, establishing a critical
legal framework for the sustainable use and conservation of plant genetic diversity.
Since 2006, Mongolia has been utilizing the IUCN Red List categories and criteria
to evaluate animal and plant species, in addition to enhancing the legal framework.
This assessment serves as a critical foundation for determining the protection status
of species, the level of threat, and the development of conservation plans. This
made Mongolia the first country in Asia to evaluate vertebrate species. Consequently,
Mongolia effectively completed the second national assessment and Red List
compilation for amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and fish in 2025, which included the
assessment of their conservation status and evaluation.
Mongolia has effectively expanded the network of protected areas, enhanced
ecological
integrity,
created
connectivity
corridors,
and
strengthened
their
management in order to protect critically endangered and endangered species, their
habitats, and distribution abundance. Nine linear infrastructure standards have been
adopted and implemented to support the protection of migratory wild animals, and
three plant species protection standards have been established.
Ecological and socio-economic assessments were updated for 144 mammal species,
513 bird species, and 78 fish species in 2023, and for 2,014 vascular plant species,
11 fungi species, and 25 moss species in 2022.
Under this objective, the Revenue from the Use of Natural Resources (RUNR) in 2025
amounted to MNT 200,496.0 million, with 25.8% of the total being allocated to
environmental protection and ecosystem restoration. 43.3% of these expenditures
were allocated to land protection, 33.7% to water resources, 11.3% to forests, and
11.6% to wildlife conservation activities. Approximately MNT 2.5 billion was allocated

Implementation of National Target 4 has advanced primarily through large-scale Red
List–aligned assessments and targeted conservation actions for threatened species
and genetic resources. Across major taxonomic groups, Mongolia reports completed
assessments for thousands of taxa using IUCN Red List categories and criteria,
alongside the adoption of standards/methodological guidance and the initiation of
species-focused measures (including in situ and ex situ efforts) to reduce extinction
risk and support genetic resource conservation. Assessment quality and trend
detection are constrained by data gaps, notably the lack of long-term monitoring
and insufficient information on distribution and population size for a number of
species. These limitations reduce the accuracy of Red List reassessments and
complicate efforts to conserve genetic diversity effectively. Although legal and policy
instruments, standards, and methodological documents have been adopted, both
files highlight that monitoring, evaluation, and compliance in practice remain
insufficient, including uneven application of approved standards and weak
coordination for field-level delivery.

To reach this goal, the following steps have been taken:
The Minister of Environment and Tourism signed Order A/208 on April 18, 2025, giving
the green light to the National Plan for the Conservation of Critically Endangered and
Endangered Species. As part of this plan, surveys were done on the size, abundance,
and distribution of significant species, such as the Gobi bear (Ursus arctos gobiensis),
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia), Przewalski’s horse (Equus ferus przewalskii), Khulan
(Equus
hemionus),
Argali
(Ovis
ammon),
Musk
deer
(Moschus
moschiferus),
Mongolian saiga (Saiga tatarica mongolica), Bactrian Camel (Camelus ferus), and Red
deer (Cervus elaphus).
A new breeding center was built outside of the Bactrian camel's natural habitat to
help the population recover. These centers now have breeding herds of about 40
animals each, which helps the population develop and the species recover.
The biological resources of about 300 species of vascular plants were looked at
in the Khangai, Khentei, and Mongolian Daura regions as part of the Government
Action Programs 2020–2024 and 2024–2028. Additionally, genetic, morphological,
and distribution research was performed on highly endangered plant species,
including Adonis mongolica, Fritillaria dagana, Saussurea involucrata, and Allium
altaicum, leading to the formulation of conservation recommendations based on the
results.
Under the “Sustainable Landscape and Biodiversity Conservation of the Dry Steppe of
Eastern Mongolia” project (2021–2026), conservation actions were implemented for
critically endangered and endangered species such as the Mongolian gazelle, goitered

gazelle, and white-naped crane.
The "Ensuring Mongolia's Native Ecosystem Resilience and Stability (Ensure)" project
(2019–2025) also preserved the habitats of severely endangered and endangered
species such the musk deer (Moschus moschiferus), red deer (Cervus elaphus),
Mongolian marmot (Marmota sibirica), and Rheum ribes.
Between 2018 and 2025, the “Future of Snow Leopard Landscapes” Project
implemented by the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) focused on protecting the
habitat of snow leopards in the Darviin Mountains and Khasagt Khairkhan areas of
Gobi-Altai Province, increasing the populations of prey species, and reducing illegal
hunting and wildlife trade. Under the project, activities were successfully carried out
with the involvement of local communities and herders, including the deployment of
livestock Bankhar dogs, installation of wildlife-friendly enclosures, implementation of
sustainable pasture management, protection of springs and water sources, and
reintroduction of marmots. These measures reduced livestock losses and increased
populations of wild animals, leading to improved snow leopard habitat, enhanced
tourism opportunities, and a comprehensive program supporting sustainable local
development, community livelihoods, and ecosystem connectivity.
Under the “Chuluut Tul” Project, implemented to restore fish populations, over an
eight-year period, 3,030,000 juvenile lenok and Mongolian grayling (Thymallus
brevirostris) were bred and released into their natural habitats. Since 2019, Mongolian
and Swedish researchers have conducted the first study of Mongolian grayling
migration in Khar Us Lake and have been working to develop policies to protect the
habitats and migratory corridors of migratory fish species, including taimen, lenok
and pike in the Nomrog and Onon river basins.
The “eZagas” electronic system, which consolidates information on fishing permits
and approved fishing zones, has been introduced and implemented in 31 soums of
Khentii and Khuvsgul provinces.
Within the framework of snow leopard conservation activities, organizations including
the Snow Leopard Trust, Snow Leopard Mongolia Center, WWF Mongolia Program,
Wildlife Conservation Society, and the Institute of Biology of the Mongolian Academy
of Sciences, together with local communities and herder cooperatives, have been
implementing initiatives to strengthen local capacities, support livelihoods, and
enhance knowledge and awareness.

Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 15 – “Protect, restore, and promote
sustainable use of terrestrial ecosystems”
• 15.5: Conserve critically endangered and endangered species of flora and
fauna, and prevent their extinction.
Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD):
• Target 4: Reduce the risk of species extinction caused by human activities.
• Target 12: Conserve genetic diversity.
Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna
and Flora (CITES):
• Supports national programs to restrict and monitor illegal trade, export, and
use of Mongolia’s rare and critically endangered species.
Ramsar Convention:
• Protects rare species of waterbirds and wetland flora and fauna and
conserves their habitats in wetland ecosystems.
Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals
(CMS):
• Supports the management and conservation of Mongolia’s migratory rare
species.
National Policies:
• Mongolia’s Sustainable Development Vision–2030:
◦15.4.3: Protect biodiversity and maintain ecosystem balance.
◦15.4.4: Conserve critically endangered and threatened species.
• Mongolia’s National Climate Change Adaptation Plan (2021–2030):
Focuses on protecting genetic diversity and mitigating climate change risks.
• State Policy on Environment (2014–2030): Emphasizes ecosystem
sustainability and protection of genetic resources.

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, register, control, and assess the impacts of invasive alien species, while
building the capacity to combat and prevent their adverse effects.
reportedActions:
SDG 15: “Protect, restore, and promote the sustainable use of terrestrial
ecosystems”
●
Target 15.8: By 2030, take measures to reduce the impacts of invasive alien
species of foreign origin, limit their spread, and implement eradication actions.
CBD: Target 6: By 2030, reduce the impacts of invasive alien species by 50%,
prevent their spread into high-risk areas, and implement effective control and
eradication measures.
IPPC: Regulates the protection of plants and plant products from pests and diseases,
ensures food safety, safeguards the environment, and promotes safe international
trade.
Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety: Regulates biosecurity risks associated with the
transboundary movement, handling, and release of genetically modified organisms
(GMOs) and biotechnology products.
“Mongolia’s Sustainable Development Vision 2030” – Section 4.4.3: Aims to reduce
ecosystem degradation, restore ecosystems, and prevent the spread of alien
species.
“National Biodiversity Conservation Program” (2015): Supports the development of
alien species inventory, monitoring, and eradication capacity, in alignment with
national objectives.
progressItems.progressSummary:

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, reduce pollution from all sources to levels that are not harmful to biodiversity
and ecosystem functions and human health.
reportedActions:
Investments have improved solid-waste management infrastructure and services in
provincial centers and Ulaanbaatar, including sanitary landfill capacity and facilities
for construction and demolition waste processing, with additional landfill planning in
key tourism areas. Monitoring indicates continuing pollution risks (e.g., pesticide
residues and contaminated agricultural land), and research has confirmed
microplastic pollution in Lake Khuvsgul and the Tuul River basin. Recycling rates
remain low and plastic waste is increasing.
Way forward: strengthen enforcement and risk-based monitoring; expand source
separation and recycling; and apply “polluter pays” and extended producer
responsibility approaches supported by digital tracking and multi-stakeholder
engagement.

With grant support from the Japan Fund for Poverty Reduction (JFPR), the “Solid
Waste Management” (G9206) project established and commissioned core waste
infrastructure in provincial centers, including centralized waste facilities, recyclable
collection points, and compaction/transfer equipment in Sukhbaatar, Darkhan-Uul,
Uvurkhangai, and Govi-Altai aimag centers, thereby improving the quality of solid
waste services. In Ulaanbaatar, a sanitary landfill with a capacity to receive 8.5 million
tons of waste in an environmentally sound manner was developed, and a construction
and demolition waste processing plant with an annual capacity of 170,000 tons was
established. In addition, under the Asian Development Bank project on sustainable
tourism development, plans were prepared to construct landfill facilities in tourism
areas, including Lake Khövsgöl and the Onon-Balj National Park, further strengthening
solid waste management infrastructure and service delivery.
To
improve
the
financial
sustainability
of
waste
services,
a
methodology
for
calculating waste service fees and a legal guidance manual for the sector were
developed. Training for public inspectors was also organized, strengthening local-level
oversight and implementation capacity.
Under the SWITCH-Asia Programme, the “Sustainable Plastic Recycling in Mongolia
(SPRIM)” project supported policy implementation on the 3R principle and sustainable
production and consumption by establishing national standards for plastic recycling,
including MNS ISO 15270:2024 and MNS ISO 16869:2024.
Evidence on chemical pollution pressures has expanded through baseline research
and monitoring. In 2022, the Institute of Plant Protection conducted a study on
“Determining the quality and residues of pesticides and fertilizers,” analyzing
residues in crop products and soil samples. Residues were detected in 30% of
imported vegetable samples, and 10% exceeded permissible limits. The 2023 land
damage report recorded damage on 82,774.5 ha of cropland nationwide, of which
7,542.1 ha (9%) was reported as contaminated by chemicals-demonstrating tangible
pressure from chemical pollution in soils and providing baseline evidence for
agricultural chemical risk assessment and monitoring.
To progressively reduce wastewater pollution and associated environmental impacts,
protect overall water resources, and promote safe water reuse, “the Law on Water
Contamination Fees” was adopted on 17 May 2012, with amendments introduced
in 2015, 2017, 2019, 2022, and 2024, alongside approval of necessary regulatory
instruments-indicating
that
wastewater
regulation
and
pollution-reduction
investments are ongoing. To strengthen implementation, a joint order dated 3
September 2025 (A/705 and A/205) approved “benchmark pollutant concentrations”
for entities discharging less than 50 m³/day of wastewater.

Under the second compact agreement between the Government of Mongolia and
the Millennium Challenge Corporation (Compact II), a wastewater recycling plant has
been constructed as part of the “Ulaanbaatar Water Supply Expansion Program.”
In addition, the “Project to expand, rehabilitate, and newly construct provincial
wastewater treatment plants” is being implemented in Bayan-Ölgii, Uvs, Zavkhan,
and Govisümber aimags, with construction works, client supervision, and testing
activities underway.
The zoning and coverage of protected areas for safeguarding aquatic ecosystems
from pollution have expanded. In 2023, 7,202,380.7 ha equivalent to 50% of
“headwater catchment areas and surface water resources” were brought under state
special protection. Mapping and methodological work developed by the World-Wide
Fund for Nature (WWF) has provided an important basis for delineating pollution-
protection zones for water bodies and wetlands.
Baseline data on pollution risks continue to grow, and research findings are emerging.
For example, a study in Lake Khövsgöl identified 20,264 microplastic particles per
km², confirming the risk of microplastic pollution and serving as a baseline indicator
for future monitoring. Research in the Tuul River Basin has also examined the impacts
of plastic, microplastic, and construction polystyrene foam waste, indicating potential
accumulation in water, sediments, and microorganisms and associated adverse
effects.
Nationally, approximately 2.2 million tons of recyclable (secondary raw material)
waste are generated annually, of which 1.4 million tons are generated in Ulaanbaatar.
Nationwide, only 3–5% of total waste is recycled, while the recycling rate in
Ulaanbaatar is 8.9%. In recent years, the volume of plastic waste has increased
year by year, and its environmental impacts have continued to rise. Plastic product
waste accounts for 26.6% of recycled waste, underscoring the need to intensify
reduction and recycling policies. Strengthening the legal framework to operationalize
the principles of “producer responsibility” and “polluter pays”-including take-back
mechanisms for single-use plastic packaging through producers, importers, and
recyclable collection points-is essential. Going forward, institutionalizing monitoring
for microplastics, chemicals, and soil pollution; harmonizing national-level databases
and reporting standards; and combining market-based incentives, digital monitoring,
and multi-stakeholder participation will increase the effectiveness of achieving the
target.

Under a project implemented by the Institute of Chemistry and Chemical Technology,
Mongolian Academy of Sciences in cooperation with the Ministry of Environment and
Tourism, with funding from the United Nations Environment Programme, a training
and seminar was held on 20 October 2023 with the participation of more than 90
national and local representatives. This activity strengthened knowledge and capacity
on the classification, analysis, and oversight of hazardous waste.
The database of toxic and hazardous chemicals has been digitalized, improving
transparency and providing a foundation for strengthening permitting and compliance
processes. In 2023, 196 enterprises and organizations obtained special permits for
toxic and hazardous chemicals through the “e-Mongolia” system.
With financing from the EU SWITCH-Asia II Programme, the project “Ensuring
Sustainable Plastic Recycling in Mongolia” was implemented to reduce waste
generation
in
target
areas
and
improve
waste
management
through
“source
separation and recycling”, including by establishing a sustainably operating central
hub. Recycling companies actively participating in the project collected and recycled
a total of 30,745 tons of waste during 2020–2024. The designation of “World
Environment Day 2025” as a call for solutions to plastic pollution is further
contributing momentum to achieving this target.
By the joint order of the Minister of Environment and Tourism, the Minister of Food,
Agriculture and Light Industry, and the Minister of Health dated 26 February 2024
(Joint Orders A/96, A/104 and A/81), the list and application rates of 252 types of
pesticides used in agriculture (57 insecticides, 128 herbicides, 62 fungicides, and
5 rodenticides) and 62 types of chemical fertilizers were approved. This provides a
policy basis for standardizing pesticide and fertilizer use in agriculture and reducing
risks of soil and water pollution arising from over-application.
Based on the results of surface water quality monitoring conducted during 2021–2023
at 193 monitoring points across 94 rivers and 19 lakes nationwide, 28–45% of the
monitored rivers and lakes were classified as “very clean”, 43–62% as “clean”,
5–12% as “slightly polluted”, 2–3% as “polluted”, 1–2% as “dirty”, and 2–3% as
“heavily polluted”. Sites classified as “polluted” included Songino, Khadan Khiasaa
and Altanbulag along the Tuul River; Khiagt in the Selenge River basin; and the
Khangal River in Orkhon Province. Sites classified as “slightly polluted” included
Shuvuun Fabrik, Selbe and Dundgol on the Tuul River system; Khangal and Chingel

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, minimize the impact of climate change on biodiversity and increase its
resilience through mitigation, adaptation, and disaster risk reduction actions through nature-
based solution and ecosystem-based approaches.

By 2030, reduce ecosystem degradation by supporting the development of sustainable,
highly productive forestry and agriculture, while introducing nature-based practices.

By 2030, increase the benefits of nature to people through ecosystem services derived
from nature-based solutions.
reportedActions:
The concept of ecosystem services (e.g., water provision, soil protection, climate
regulation, food and raw materials, and cultural values) has begun to be integrated
into policy and planning, with strengthened legal and policy foundations. The National
Adaptation Plan (NAP) includes provisions to protect and restore water-related
ecosystem services. Work has been undertaken to introduce methodologies for
ecosystem service valuation at the level of protected areas and river basins, compile
baseline information, and prepare assessment and research reports. Pilot ecosystem
service valuations were carried out during 2019–2023 in Bayankhongor, Govi-Altai,
Bulgan, and Khentii aimags, and were incorporated into local development plans,
marking
an
initial
step
toward
using
valuation
results
in
decision-making.
A
methodology was also developed to estimate the total value of forest ecosystem
services, including the value of forest resources and non-timber forest products as
well as indirect benefits-covering seven service categories: protecting forests, water,
soils, and biodiversity; carbon storage; and recreation.

In Mongolia, economic incentives for sustainable natural resource use and financing
sources for conservation and restoration have been established through regulatory
instruments such as land fees, air pollution charges, and fees for the use of water and
mineral springs, forests, wildlife, and natural plant resources. “The Law on Natural
Resource Use Fees” sets fee rates for the use of resources including plants, water
and mineral springs, forests, and wildlife, and establishes provisions for allocating a
defined share of fee revenues to environmental protection and restoration measures.
Related regulations and ecological–economic valuation methodologies have also been
updated and are being implemented. However, the allocation and use of fee revenues
for environmental protection and restoration in line with legal and regulatory
requirements has not been fully implemented, posing a constraint to sustainable
financing.
In 2020, the Asia Foundation conducted a study on the feasibility of calculating
ecosystem service payments in “green zones,” forest and water fund areas, and
their protection zones, including an assessment of international experts. Researchers
from the Physical Geography Division of the Institute of Geography and Geoecology,
Mongolian Academy of Sciences carried out a study on determining the ecosystem
value of the Lake Khövsgöl Strictly Protected Area and calculating ecosystem service
payments, developing a methodology for estimating ecosystem service values. Other
domestic and international researchers have also been undertaking studies in this
field.
As part of piloting ecosystem service payment mechanisms, initiatives have been
implemented in project target areas to protect rangeland ecosystems, reduce
degradation, and support restoration through: (1) providing incentives for livestock
sales to herder households that reduce herd sizes to match pasture carrying capacity;
and (2) establishing a “Risk Fund” to support the implementation of five-year
integrated plans of herder groups. Following pilot implementation of livestock-sale
incentives with 225 herder groups, end-of-year livestock census results for 2022
showed a 23.4% reduction in total livestock numbers—10.1 percentage points higher
than among non-participating herders. Building on this initiative, Bayantsagaan soum
of Bayankhongor aimag continued the pilot in 2023, and as a result 614 herder
households across 17 herder groups reduced their livestock by 160.2 thousand sheep
units, thereby relieving grazing pressure and freeing up pasture areas.

Under air pollution reduction policies, regulatory and enforcement measures have
been implemented to improve fuel use and modernize heating devices, phase out
non-compliant equipment, and strengthen compliance with standards. Nationwide,
the fixed air quality monitoring network has been expanded, the capacity of
automatic stations has been increased, and data flows have been improved.
Projects to protect drinking water sources and upgrade water supply networks in
both urban and rural areas have been implemented, alongside measures to improve
access to safe drinking water. To protect urban water resources, solutions for reusing
treated wastewater, including for industrial uses such as thermal power plants have
been piloted, and related infrastructure upgrades are underway.
Overall, Mongolia has established a foundation for maintaining and restoring nature’s
contributions to people by supporting ecosystem conservation, sustainable use, and
local participation.

progressItems.targetText: By 2030, Integrate biodiversity issues into the policies and planning of all sectors.
reportedActions:
Mongolia is implementing the following key measures to integrate biodiversity (BD)
into cross-sectoral policies and planning:
• The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) (2015–2025) has been
approved and is under implementation, serving as the core policy document for
aligning biodiversity conservation with national development policies.
• Initial steps have been taken to integrate biodiversity conservation into the policies
of sectors beyond the environment sector, including agriculture, livestock, and
forestry, where natural resource use is dominant.
• The System of Environmental-Economic Accounting (SEEA) has been piloted since
2018
with
the
support
of
UNESCAP,
creating
an
initial
foundation
for
using
quantitative natural resource data in policy and decision-making. In this context,
the Ministry of Environment and Climate Change, the Ministry of Mining and Heavy
Industry, and the Agency for Land Administration, Geodesy and Cartography have
been conducting partial natural resource accounts.
• The Law on Fees for the Use of Natural Resources explicitly defines funding sources
for environmental protection, thereby establishing a legal framework to improve the
linkage between resource use and conservation.
• Mongolia’s accession as an associate member to the Global Biodiversity Information
Facility (GBIF) has enhanced opportunities to collect, use, and apply national
biodiversity data in policy formulation in accordance with international standards.
•
The
National
“One
Health”
Strategy
was
approved
in
2022,
reflecting
the
interlinkages between environmental, human, and animal health at the policy level,
representing a significant advancement in jointly addressing biodiversity loss, climate
change, and zoonotic disease risks.
• Research conducted by the Mongolian Academy of Sciences (2021–2024) identified
that water scarcity in the Gobi and desert regions, degradation of green zones, and
wildlife migration constitute underlying risk factors for the transmission of infectious
diseases, providing important scientific evidence for evidence-based policymaking.
• The adoption of the Law on Development Policy, Planning and Its Management
(2020) established a legal framework for ensuring coherence and an integrated
monitoring and evaluation system across long-, medium-, and short-term national
development policies.

progressItems.targetText:
By 2030, establish systems to monitor and transparently report the impacts, risks, and
outcomes of business activities regarding biodiversity.

By 2030, minimize overconsumption and waste through supporting public education on
sustainable consumption.

By 2030, enhance the legislative, governance, and monitoring systems for genetically
modified organisms.

By 2030, reform subsidies and incentives that have negative impacts on biodiversity,
while increasing environmentally positive (green) incentives.

Substantially and progressively increase financial resources towards biodiversity
conservation from all sources, in an effective, timely, innovative and easily accessible manner.

Strengthen capacity-building and development, access to and transfer of technology,

and promote development of and access to innovation and technical and scientific cooperation
in biodiversity conservation.

By 2030, data and information relevant to biodiversity and ecosystem services are
widely accessible to decision makers, scientists and the public to guide effective and equitable
governance, integrated and participatory management of biodiversity.

By 2030, ensure full, equitable, inclusive, effective, and gender-responsive
representation and participation in decision-making and implementation related to biodiversity
and ensure rights over relevant resources of local communities, women and girls as well as
youth.
